claims.text: Residual internal stress and strain localized at interfaces and grain boundaries dominate the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis of as-deposited nanoscale non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi films.
Interfacial and grain-boundary strain induces defect-mediated magnetic-domain pinning.
Defect-mediated domain pinning produces less reversible and broadened field-induced phase transitions.
Rapidly deposited nanoscale films or nanoribbons typically contain non-equilibrium residual stresses, interface defects, and grain-boundary strains.
A controlled moderate-temperature anneal can relieve internal stress without causing significant coarsening or undesired phase transformations.
An annealing temperature of 100–200 °C is below the bulk recrystallization threshold for the relevant material.
The permissible magnetic-cooling cycle frequency is limited by heat-transfer rates.
Annealing reduces residual internal stress and interfacial defect density.
Reducing residual stress and defect density diminishes domain-wall pinning.
Reduced domain-wall pinning enhances the reversibility of magnetic-field-driven phase transitions.
Reduced domain-wall pinning lowers hysteresis and sharpens the magnetocaloric transition.
Lower hysteresis and a sharper transition produce a more efficient magnetic-cooling cycle.
Annealed films will have a lower hysteresis-loop area than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealed films will exhibit a sharper and more reversible magnetic transition than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealed films will exhibit a modestly greater temperature change per cycle than the as-deposited baseline.
As-deposited films have significant hysteresis and suboptimal magnetocaloric performance because of high residual stress and defect-induced domain pinning.
The proposed mechanism applies to films or nanoribbons no thicker than 100 nm under applied fields below 1 T.
The proposed effect may not extrapolate to bulk or highly recrystallized structures.
